I have to agree with agentzero on this one. Presence already has
a huge advantage in political actions. In fact, the only consistently
viable voting deck is one that uses Presence.

One might make a case for a Malkavian deck using Anarch Revolt
and Malkavian Rider Clause, but that's a rather specialized way
to do it.

The reasoning that weenie political decks are unusually powerful
with the previous errata (you can vote-push with any and all PA
cards in your hand, but could not replace them until the end of
your turn) is incredibly naive. For example:

1) A weenie deck that depends on the 8 votes (replace the
action card but not the ones spent to vote pushed) will only be
able to get one political action to pass.

2) It is incredibly easy to intercept weenie voters. You can get +1
intercept so easily, it's sick.

3) They have no combat defense whatsoever. Rush decks
will rip them apart like tissue.

4) They have no bleed defense. A good stealth bleed deck will oust
them in no time flat.

5) A "real" voting deck will shut them down. Even with the previous
errta, Awe, Bewitching Oration and Dread Gaze control the political
arena. A weenie political deck at least made another political deck
have to work harder.

There were several things that I thought were huge blunders that came
out of 7/7. This was one of the biggest.

It's strange (to me) that you feel this way, since this is one of the
oldest rules that was 'officialized' with the 7/7 rulings. In the ancient
Sensible Player's Tournament Rules (SPTR), the two basic principles were
(1) No Limits (no per-card limit on anything) and (2) Golden Tenets (no
repeat actions, no vote push).

Many playgroups have been using the no-vote-push rule for years. It does
give Presence-using vote decks a significant advantage over non-Presence
using vote decks. However, the feeling among SPTR-using players has
always been that Presence ought to be a benefit for vote decks just as
Obfuscate is a benefit for stealth-bleed decks. It is not possible for a deck
to gain any significant amount of stealth without using disciplined cards -
why should it be possible for a deck to gain substantial votes without
using a discipline?

Furthermore, note that Bribes is disciplineless but helps pass votes -
analogous to Computer Hacking.

> One might make a case for a Malkavian deck using Anarch Revolt
> and Malkavian Rider Clause, but that's a rather specialized way
> to do it.

Funny, though. ^_^ (I assume that you're referring to playing AR,
and when someone calls a vote to burn it, let it pass and then Malk Rider
Clause it... hilarious!)

> The reasoning that weenie political decks are unusually powerful
> with the previous errata (you can vote-push with any and all PA
> cards in your hand, but could not replace them until the end of
> your turn) is incredibly naive. For example:

Actually, it was based on tournament experience, to the best of my
knowledge.

> 1) A weenie deck that depends on the 8 votes (replace the
> action card but not the ones spent to vote pushed) will only be
> able to get one political action to pass.

If the first one is a Praxis Seizure, you can start passing a great many
votes with your second turn.

> 2) It is incredibly easy to intercept weenie voters. You can get +1
> intercept so easily, it's sick.

Sick? Shouldn't this shut down presence voters even better since they
don't have as many vamps available to call votes? Also, intercept decks
seem to perform poorly enough in tournament settings that you can rely
on not seeing very many of them in actual tourneys.

> 3) They have no combat defense whatsoever. Rush decks
> will rip them apart like tissue.

Only Immortal Grapple decks. Dodge is disciplineless. And weenie decks
can be difficult for rush decks, just because they can get out so many
vampires.

> 4) They have no bleed defense. A good stealth bleed deck will oust
> them in no time flat.

A good weenie vote-push deck will oust its prey rather faster than a good
standard Malk-type stealth bleed deck will oust it. You don't need bleed
defense if you can sweep the table fast enough.

> 5) A "real" voting deck will shut them down. Even with the previous
> errta, Awe, Bewitching Oration and Dread Gaze control the political
> arena. A weenie political deck at least made another political deck
> have to work harder.

In my experience, anti-vote reactions, especially the vote-gaining ones,
are not very widely used. This is because there are almost always more
productive things to put in the card slots, which don't rely on your
opponents playing vote decks.

Bewitching Oration and especially Awe will help a presence voter to pass
its votes (Awe is a bit on the Just Wrong side in my estimation), sure,
but they won't do much toward keeping the weenie from passing his votes
unless you're also calling lots of Praxis Seizures. And if the weenie
has gotten a quick enough start on the PS action, they may be able to
outvote you from the outset. Even if not, dumping a hand of political
actions can often stop even a Bewitching Oration-ed vote, unless the
Presence player already has titles on the table.

> There were several things that I thought were huge blunders that came
> out of 7/7. This was one of the biggest.

This was one of the most widely used before 7/7... In many groups, this
rule is considered the very essence of balance.

Josh

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 6 Nov 1998 Dhar...@yahoo.com wrote:

> agentzero wrote:
> > Even after extensive play using this ruling, I still feel that it is
> > very retarded and only serves to severely restrict all vote decks.
>
> I have to agree with agentzero on this one. Presence already has
> a huge advantage in political actions. In fact, the only consistently
> viable voting deck is one that uses Presence.

Their has been debate on this before, but since it has come up again, I
shall post some thoughts I had on the subject from an earlier private
E-mail discussion, where I argued against the idea that the old way made
voting less predictable:

----------------------------

I like "no vote push".

I have a strong bias towards in favor of following the official rules.
But I have other reasons for liking some sort of "no vote push" rule:

One is the versatility and variety it promotes. Jyhad is full of
interesting vote modifiers and vote reactions. Many rarely saw play under
the old way, because it was so easy just to stuff your hand with Political
Action cards and play them with total versatility either as 1) vote action
cards, 2) vote modifiers gaining votes for votes you cast, 3) vote
reaction cards gaining votes in other peoples votes. With the old system,
there is no need to agonize about how many PA cards to play as opposed
to vote modifiers, or vote reactions. You can simply throw in all PA
cards and use them for all 3 purposes.

With vote push eliminated, one must compensate with other strategies,
like:

Presence Voting (Charming Lobby, Bewitching Oration, Dread Gaze,
Business Pressure)
Having large titled vampires
Hosing large titled vampires (Command of Harpies, eg)
Having the Edge when voting
Surprise Influence
Having vote Locations (Ventrue HQ, Elesium PV, etc.)
Hosing vote locations (Arson, Disputed Territory, Unnatural
Disaster, Kine Dominance.)
Regaining the Upper Hand (built-in "cryptic rider" of one
extra vote on your next vote this turn--the only real
point the card ever had, but it is pointless if you can
just use the card for a vote push anyway.)
Bribes (Surprisingly Effective)
Cryptic Rider
Delaying Tactics
Elder Kindred Network
Pulling Strings
Kindred Coercion
Scorn of Adonis
Telepathic Vote Counting
Votes that can enlist support from other Methuselahs, (like
Ancient Influence, Parity Shift, Rumors of Gehenna)
Justicar siezure PAs (followed by Cryptic Riders, perhaps)
Closed Session
Conflict of Interests
Of Noble Blood (vote-free Primogen siezure)
Malkavian Rider Clause

Many of the above will never see play because they are just not effective
alternatives to a hand full of PAs. Now you might say that "Surprise
Influence" is a better card than a PA because it gives you 2 votes
instead of 1, but consider the following.

-- You can get rid of the PA any time you want. A handful of PAs
will not cause hand jam.
-- You do not need an untapped minion (or any minion at all) to
play the PA
-- A PA can be played as an action card to call a vote
-- A PA can be used to add modify your own vote action, like an
action modifier

All in all, you'd be almost crazy to put in Surprise Influence when you
could put in a couple of PA's instead. A similar analysis would apply to
most vote modifiers and reactions. These cards become wallpaper, with
PA's serving both functions as well as their primary one. Only the best
vote modifiers (the presence vote modifiers) ever see play, because a
handful of PAs is so much more versatile. Under "vote push" PAs are
broken cards that invalidate 2 whole other classes of cards.

Arguably, the "no-vote push" situation is what was originally intended by
the Jyhad rulebook. See page 39.

"A political card always provides one vote for the Methuselah
playing it. This card is immediately replaced after being played.
Additional political cards can also be used by any of the other
Methuselahs for votes. The actual effects of these cards are
ignored. Cards used in this way are discarded to the ash heap and
not replaced until the voting is finished."

This passage seems to be saying that burning additional cards for
additional votes is something *other* Methuselahs can do, not the one
calling the vote. At the time, though, the RT ruled otherwise.
Nonetheless, many argued for years that that was what it should have been.
I tend to agree.

If you want to make things unpredictable, why not allow unlimited PA vote
playing by the *other* Methuselahs, as seems consistent with the above
text. This would also make it even harder for Weenies to become Princes,
which, one might argue, is a more faithful representation of the WOD
universe. (I am not convinced, though, that this is demonstrably better
than the current official way.)

But there is no reason to allow vote pushing by acting Methuselahs, if you
want to promote unpredictability. There is nothing unpredictable about
weenies pushing praxis siezures with a handful of PAs on their first turn.
It is boring, and makes weenie vote much too powerful.

On the net, some people argued against the new rule, saying that "Presence
Voting" would now be the only viable voter deck type. Experienced players
who have using the "no vote push" rule for years, however, say that
promotes greater variety in vote deck types. It only hurts weenie vote
decks, which needed to be curbed and remain powerful nonetheless.

Lupus Australis

On Fri, 6 Nov 1998 Dhar...@yahoo.com wrote:

> > Even after extensive play using this ruling, I still feel that it is

> I have to agree with agentzero on this one.

No offense to agentzero, but I would translate his statement as "it only
serves to severely retard all severely retarded vote decks". It does not
take alot of brains, skill, creativity or strategy to pack your deck with
PAs and use them willy nilly as vote actions, vote reactions that don't
require ready minions, or as discipline-free vote modifiers.
Unfortunately, under "vote push" this is so effective that any other
cards or strategies become counter productive (except for the most
effective, such as Presence modifiers).

> Presence already has
> a huge advantage in political actions. In fact, the only consistently
> viable voting deck is one that uses Presence.

Under "vote push" only the best vote modifiers and vote reactions have a
chance of competing with a hand packed full of PAs. Presence Modifiers
such as Bewitching Oration are among the few that qualify. At the risk of
oversimplifying slightly, one can say that under "Vote Push", there are
only 2 viable strategies: Presence voting and Vote Pushing.

This has caused many thoughtless people to carelessly assume that, once
you eliminate Vote Push, there will be only one strategy left: Presence
voting.

Actually, eliminating vote push creates a power vacuum that allows
alternative vote strategies a chance to compete. Even Presence voting is
cut down to size, as in the past the power of Presence votes could be
inhanced by vote pushing.

Imagine, for instance, that I want to Sieze a Praxis, and have 3 weenie
minions out: Nik, Franciscus, and Deiter Kleist. Problem: playing the
Praxis will give you only one vote, and you suspect you will need more
than that, as there is already a Biship on the table who has no reason to
vote for your becoming Prince, and there are plenty of others that
probably have vote cards in their hands. Also, your predator has the
edge, and he's not going to vote for you either. So the first thing you
do is play Cat Burglary with Nik, gaining the edge. Then you play Praxis
Siezure, tossing in the edge for a vote. The Biship votes against you and
2 other people play PA cards, so you play Telepathic Vote counting and
take the card back into your hand. Finally Deiter gives it a shot, and
modifies it with Bribes and Scorn of Adonis. This time the Bishop
abstains, one person throws a vote in your favor to benefit from the
Bribes, and only one of your opponents throws down a PA card against you,
losing a pool in the process. Your vote passes 2 - 1.

This interesting scenario would be completely ludicrous under "PA vote
push", because it would make absolutely no sense for you to have Cat
Burglary, Telepathic Vote Counting, Bribes, and Scorn of Adonis in your
hand, when you could throw these out of your deck, replace them with 4 PA
cards, and just push the vote though that way.

> One might make a case for a Malkavian deck using Anarch Revolt
> and Malkavian Rider Clause, but that's a rather specialized way
> to do it.

That is a nice creative notion. Better than 50% PAs in the deck.

> The reasoning that weenie political decks are unusually powerful
> with the previous errata (you can vote-push with any and all PA
> cards in your hand, but could not replace them until the end of
> your turn) is incredibly naive. For example:

I don't know if weenie vote push is incredibly powerful, but it is
certainly incredibly dull.

> 1) A weenie deck that depends on the 8 votes (replace the
> action card but not the ones spent to vote pushed) will only be
> able to get one political action to pass.

In my experience, a weenie deck never needs 8 votes to pass a Praxis
Siezure on its first minion phase.

> 2) It is incredibly easy to intercept weenie voters. You can get +1
> intercept so easily, it's sick.

Unless they are my fast replicating Weenie Nossie Obfuscators.
Alternatively, you might have to deal with four 1 capacity caitiff all
trying to call praxis Siezure on their first minion phase. How many of
them are you going to be able to intercept?

> 3) They have no combat defense whatsoever. Rush decks
> will rip them apart like tissue.

No one ever said such decks were unbeatable. Still, weenie decks,
including weenie vote decks, tend to win a disproportionate amount ot the
time.

Of course, my weenie Nossie obfuscators like to whip out assault rifles
with disguised weapon when they are rushed, with Behind You for additional
maneuver if necessary. They pay for these with consanguinous Boons, of
course.

> 4) They have no bleed defense. A good stealth bleed deck will oust
> them in no time flat.

Unless they oust their own prey first.

> 5) A "real" voting deck will shut them down. Even with the previous
> errta, Awe, Bewitching Oration and Dread Gaze control the political
> arena. A weenie political deck at least made another political deck
> have to work harder.

Dread Gaze is rarely played, because "vote push" is more versatile and
reliable. Bewitching oration will have no effect on *your* votes.

> There were several things that I thought were huge blunders that came
> out of 7/7. This was one of the biggest.

I could not disagree more.

to do it."

Or, make a deck out of princes. Or make an Auspex deck (probably a Malk
Stealth/Vote deck) that uses Telepathic Vote Counting (a pretty strong vote
card). Or use Bribes. Or convince your allies across the table to vote for
you. Politics are not meant to be completely one sided. Before the offical no
vote push rules, voting tended to be completely one sided--politicking had no
effect, cause _any_ vote deck could push their vote through by tossing votes
away. Now, only a Presence deck (or a deck with titled vampires) can do this,
and other political decks have to be, well, political. I fail to see how this
is a bad thing. If you want to make a vote superiority/lock down deck, use
either Presence or large, titled vampires (probably backed by rampant pool
gain). If you are not happy with these options for whatever reason (like you
wan't stealth), you trade a less certain vote lock for increased abilities
elsewhere, like stealth.

"The reasoning that weenie political decks are unusually powerful
with the previous errata (you can vote-push with any and all PA
cards in your hand, but could not replace them until the end of
your turn) is incredibly naive. For example:"

No, this is not naive at all. As has been shown for years at many, many
tournaments, the weenie vote push deck was too powerful. This last year at
Origins, the WVP deck was highly successful, losing the finals due to table
position. WVP was such a well recognized problem that it directly resulted in
the poorly designed original Card Limit tourney rules, the second wave "limited
vote push rules", the superior "Sensible Persons Tournament Rules", and finally
the official "no vote push" rules. There is so much evidence that points to
the fact that unrestricted vote cycling is too powerful that some sort of fix
was inevitable, and the current one works fine.

"There were several things that I thought were huge blunders that came out of
7/7. This was one of the biggest."

The No Vote Push rules did not come out of the 7/7 rules. They are arguably
how the rules were inteded to work in the first place, and were one of the
original common house rules fixes. My group has been playing with the very
same rules for years now, as have many other groups, and as such, a great deal
of "playtesting" of the No Vote Push rules have been done for a very long time.

Please don't take this as a jab, as it is in no way meant to be, but as your
group regularly uses 6CL, it seems unlikely that you have had all that much
experience with Tourney designed WVP decks (I could be completely wrong, and
you could go to sanctioned tourneys every week, however...). A WVP deck with
only 6 KRC and 6 ConAG is going to be _much_ less effective than a WVP deck
with 15 of each, and as such, I can see why you wouldn't think it was a
problem.

On Sat, 7 Nov 1998, James Coupe wrote:

> >All in all, you'd be almost crazy to put in Surprise Influence when you
> >could put in a couple of PA's instead.
>

> Not necessarily. Many people *do* leave a vampire untapped and ready at
> the end of their minion phase as a blocker (or whatever they intend to
> react with). Also, card space.

I think you are overestimating the inportance of the "card space" issue as
it applies to this situation. There are very few decks that use all their
"card space" in the course of a game.

In practice, especially under old vote push rules, a surprise influence
takes up far more space in your *hand* than will an equivalent or greater
number of PAs because you cannot burn through the Surprise Influences as
quickly and easily as the PAs. The card has a high opportunity cost,
which will slow down your deck and game, and in the end result in your
casting fewer votes and having less influence. Having twice as many votes
in your deck will not help you if you move through the deck only half as
fast.

Imagine I have a 90 card deck with 20 PA cards in it. If I want, I can
replace those 20 cards with 10 Surprise influences. The result is a
smaller deck (80 cards) with the same number of votes. However, the 90
card deck will be far more fluid, and burn through a greater number of
cards, and votes, in the course of the game. In neither case will running
out of cards be likely to be an issue.

Of course, I could replace my 20 PA cards with 20 Surprise Influences,
making full use of available "deck space". This, however, will only
compound my troubles. My deck will be slower than ever, with most SIs
being played during the discard phase. The deck with the PAs will still
end up casting more votes and having more influence.

Now you may argue that this is a bad hypothetical example because no-one
would devise a strategy solely out of SI. Fair enough, but the argument
is still valid no matter what combination of high opportunity vote
modifiers and vote reactions I put in my deck to replace double their
number of PAs. I've played a Toreador deck with lots of political action
modifiers in them, and believe me, it can be a real bummer when you have a
bunch of modifiers in your hand and no actions to modify -- or a bunch of
reaction cards in your hand and no-one playing votes. A handful of PAs
simply does not give you this problem (unless "no vote push" is played).

> A random Consanguineous Boon in your
> deck gives you 1 vote of vote defence. A Surprise Influence gives you 2
> votes of vote defence for the same card slottage. Granted, the PA could
> be got rid of in other ways, but for simple vote defence, it's not as
> good.

No, it's better. If I have 4 Consanguinous Boons in my hand, I can play
them all on my minion phase, replace them, and still have yet more
Consanguinous Boons to play for "Vote reactions" on other people's minion
phases. Being able to play these cards causes other cards to come up,
including perhaps that Minion Tap I've been hoping for.

If I have 2 Surprise Influences in my hand, however, I cannot use them on
my minion phase at all. I have to wait for others to cast votes on
*their* turn, and if no-one obliges I am stuck with discarding. It may be
a while before that Minion Tap I need comes up. Even if someone does cast
a vote, I can only play one SI per untapped minion. With double the
number of PAs, I could have played as many as I wanted, even with *no*
untapped minions.

Under old vote push rules, a few SIs will jam your hand far more easily
than double, triple, or even quadruple the number of PAs.

> OTOH, though, Delaying Tactics may be better still for simply
> getting rid of votes.

A good card, made even better due to NRA. Note that under "no vote push"
its disadvantage -- that it allows your opponent to get back his PA card,
is more significant, because your opponent is likely to have a more
limitted number of PA cards in his deck. Under "vote push" this was often
an advantage, because it prevented your opponent from being able to cycle
cards.

> Is vote defence simply about stopping votes going through though? Well,

> Rather than vote defence, decks should contain vote influence - the
> ability to have your say in a vote. If someone is calling a vote which

> Delaying Tactics is useless. My Surprise Influence gives me more votes
> to aid them than my Consanguineous Boon would, but like you say, my
> Consanguineous Boon gives me more flexibility.

Again, I disagree. The Consanguinous Boons would gain you more votes
because you would get to play more of them.

>
> You know, it seems to me that if what you say above is still true, then
> the 7/7 ruling has done nothing to stem WVP and only serves to restrict
> all the other Political deck types.

I fail to follow your logic. In a WVP environment, WVP dominates other
voting strategies. If another vote deck comes up against a WVP deck,
I'm saying that the regular vote deck will lose. Reason being, after
the WVP deck's second turn, he has 1 to 4 Princes. With that, he can
push the rest of his votes through because you most likely have only
one titled vampire at most plus all of your own vote cards to push. You
have 2 + 7 cards to push with for 9 votes. He has 2 + 1 from original
PA + 7 to push with for 10 votes. And this is only if he went first.
If he didn't go first, he has even more votes and needs to push with fewer
cards. If the weenie doesn't draw enough Praxis Seizures for each of
his vampires, he can just dump all the non-PS cards in his first vote
and second vote ad nauseum until he has the cards he needs. My feeling
is that the WVP doesn't get its strength from it's ability to push to
get votes to pass but from its ability to unload all the cards it wants
that it doesn't need at the moment if it so desires.

In a non-push environment, the weenie needs to draw the Praxis Seizures
it needs in its initial hand. Also, whenever it want to do a damaging
vote, it has to have it in its hand. It can't depend on swapping its hand
for a new one to get the PA's it needs. So the WVP has lost that
strength. It has also lost its strength of forcing its votes through.

Presence vote decks generally didn't stand a chance against WVP. It
took vote push to beat vote push if things actually got to a vote. With
the new ruling back basically what the original Jyhad rulebook says,
Presence vote has become the strongest vote type. Other vote decks
are still viable just as a Pro/Dom S&B deck is viable. But when it comes
to sheer output, a Presence deck can generate many more votes and a
Obfuscate based Stealth deck can generate much more stealth.

I've made several effective vote decks that didn't use Presence or
vote push. Many other people have, too. But rather than being screwed
by both WVP _AND_ Presence based votes, they only have to worry about
Presence just totally hosing them.

One final note. I think a lot of the naysayers are missing one big
advantage that vote decks of all kinds have gained. Before the ruling,
you had no idea how many votes in the form of burned PA's might come
from your opponents. Now, you know that at most 1 PA will come from
each person. Makes it a lot easier to decide if you have enough votes
to pass.

Mike

In article <F28BB...@midway.uchicago.edu>, Rachel & Chris
<reei...@midway.uchicago.edu> writes

>Direct Intervention -is- a broken card...

A very controversial remark.

First of all, I *will* concede that for many people there are reasons of
taste why it shouldn't be in the game. It smacks of counterspell which
they just don't like. Maybe it does or doesn't fit into the theme of
the game. For me, I just like the idea that, every once in a while, a
Methuselah just come out and force one of his ideas through. Other
people don't like that.

There are circumstances when the card has to be banned. In JOL
(http://www.deckserver.net) having Direct Intervention is not a
practical thing, really. Every time someone plays a card, another
person could just wait 24 hours and reverse the card. Due to it being
play-by-email, the ramifications of the card are different.

But looking at it from purely a power-cost ratio point of view. Okay,
it CAN cancel any minion card. What does that really mean? Well, if
it's stealth, it could mean you get into combat and die. If it's
intercept, it could mean my action gets through and does horrible things
to you. If it's a vote, the vote is stopped or fails (from cancelling
the Awe, say), or passes if you cancel someone else's Delaying Tactics,
say. In combat, it means someone gets hit harder.

Let's look at this the other way though. If it's stealth you want to
cancel, you can play intercept. If it's intercept you want to cancel,
play more stealth. If it's a vote you want to cancel, play Delaying
Tactics or Surprise Influence or a Vote card. If you want to pass a
vote, have more vote passing and vote cards. In combat, if it's a
maneuver that's been cancelled, play another maneuver. If it's a
strike, play Dodge. If it's damage, play Skin of Rock, or Flesh of
Marble or Flak Jacket.

So, most cards in the game have ways round them somehow or other. I can
burn cards, sew up cards (Pentex, Sensory Deprivation etc.), vote, bleed
or whatever. Each thing you do has a counter-card from my point of
view. If I'm desperately afraid of you, I'll have a few of those cards.

Now, consider Delaying Tactics. Once per turn, I can pay 1 pool to
cancel a card you play.

Once per turn - well, if I've been thoughtful and put lots of Dread
Gazes in my deck to stop your votes, I can do that several times. Or
Delaying Tactics. I can prevent your strikes multiple times (Skin of
Steel in every combat). I can intercept more of your actions if I play
proper intercept. Direct Intervention is, in many instances, a poor
man's whatever card you wanted to play.

1 pool - well, that's pretty hefty. If I play a Sport Bike, I can block
many of your actions for the same pool cost, perhaps. If I play a
Labyrinth, that's more stealth for me a lot of the time, rather than
stopping one of your intercept cards once.

Cancelling a card - Well, what can that do? One of the often heard
arguments is that "Well, it stops my plans dead." No, it doesn't, at
least, not moreso than, say, Delaying Tactics. I'm planning to call a
vote. If I call it, someone could play Delaying Tactics and I have to
plan to that effect. It's not like everything not going to plan is a
new concept. I have to, at every point, take into account that you can
smack me back, or block, or burn my location, or eat me or whatever.
Delaying Tactics provides a new, flexible way for me to do it, but it's
nothing new. You may play Immortal Grapple but I could have a Burning
Wrath hiding in my big Ventrue with Potence deck which is just as much
of a surprise as Direct Intervention would be.

Looking at it from the spoiling my plans point of view, from another
perspective, is that what Jyhad is about? Just bringing plans to
fruition and trying to stop other people. Not quite. That's what
something like the X-Files is like (Mythos, too, perhaps) - two people
playing separate games and just trying to beat the other and maybe throw
a spanner in the works from time to time. Jyhad has always been about
interaction - the voting system, the blood hunts, the ability to share
intercept and so forth have been hard encoded into the game from Day 1.

And does it really bugger up my plans? Well, if I'm playing a vote
deck, I should have enough of the votes I need to get through, expecting
that some of them will fail. If I don't, that's my tough luck. Same
with stealth etc. If it's a prayer card you've drawn (your one Arson)
then which is more unfair? You drawing a prayer card and getting a
shift in the balance of the game (perhaps heavily to you), or my
cancelling the prayer card and keeping the balance how it is?

Did you read Adrian Sullivan's article on DI and how it can take advantage

that DI becomes overpowered when it produces a very large swing effect
by stopping a card at a critical moment. For example, if you DI someone's
Majesty and thereby burn their vampire... or DI someone's Deflection, and
they are therefore ousted... that sort of thing.

if they had one. But they won't *always* have one. In my mind, DI adds

of course, to being a classic 'trump' card.) And its versatility is not
sufficiently compensated by the 1-pool cost. Consider your example of DI
vs 'prayer' cards: Is it more fair for someone to draw their prayer card
at the right time and get a big shift, or for someone to DI that prayer
card, maintaining the status quo? Notice that 'prayer' cards are by their

Noal, I think this is a weak argument. True, Obfuscate does not have *all* of
the stealth cards. Most disciplines include at least one action that is at +1
stealth. However, of the disciplines you listed above, only Protean and
Obtenebration (I believe) have more than 2 cards that are +stealth action
modifiers. Most of the other disciplines also only have +1 stealth action
modifiers.

Necromancy, for example has the +1 stealth/+1 intercept (or the
reverse...whatever...) card. That's it. As has been discussed many a time
on here, getting +1 or +2 permanent intercept is pretty easy. Many players
make a habit of including this much in *any* deck they build.

Celerity has Alacrity. +1 stealth. That's it, unless you count the "bleed
for 1, ignore excess" actions as being highly stealthy.

Vicissitude: Changeling & Plasmic Form. +1 stealth, one at inferior, the
other at superior.

Dominate has Bonding. It also has Dominate Kine as an action, or whatever, I
think. Neither really counts.

Chimerstry: Fata Morgana. +1 stealth.

Dementation: Mind Tricks. Confusion adds stealth to a bleed.

Obtenebration: Shadow Play +1/+2 stealth = Lost in Crowds. Shroud of Night
+1 stealth for non-bleeding/+1 stealth. Pretty weak.

Protean: Earth Control +1/+2 stealth = Lost in Crowds. Form of Mist...sorta.
Rapid Change: +1 stealth at inferior. Also pretty weak.

Serpentis: Form of the Serpent. +1 stealth at inferior.

Compare this all with Obfuscate's Cloak the Gathering, Faceless Night, Lost in
Crowds, Mask of 1K Faces, Psychic Veil (not an action mod, but close enough in
practice...), Spying Mission, Elder Impersonation, Forgotten Labyrinth,
Swallowed by Night...that's 9 stealth cards, plus Marked Path and Hidden
Pathways...which almost count...

Protean is the second best with about 2-and-a-half stealth cards. All told,
Obfuscate cards make up approximately half of the stealth cards in the whole
set. Now, considering that in practice, you would not likely be using more
than three or four of these disciplines at the same time (and most of them
don't match up anyway...), you would have trouble playing more than 3 or 4
action modifiers for stealth...for we all know you can't use the same card
twice on the same action. However, with Obfuscate, you can use almost all of
the above at once. Cloak + Faceless Night + Lost in Crowds + Mask of 1K Faces
+ Spying Mission + Elder Impersonation + Forgotten Labyrinth + Swallowed by
Night = (at superior) +11 stealth. Almost quadruple what the next closest
discipline can come up with. And at least double what you could come up with
any non-screwy (read: workable without lots and lots of skill cards...)
combination of the above disciplines.

Note also that there's a lot more stealth flying around than intercept.
Auspex has intercept. Auspex *is* intercept. Chimerstry has a little
intercept, 2 or 3 cards IIRC. Necromancy has that card, Spectral Divination
for +1 int at superior. It also has +1/+2 intercept vs...diablerie with Eyes
of the Dead. Big deal. Animalism has Cat's Guidance and Raptors/Raven Spies.
Obtenebration has Eyes of the night for +1 intercept. Anything else? Maybe
1 card under Vicissitude.

> The comparison simply doesn't match up. I would appreciate it if everyone
> would stop trying to use this faulty analogy. I'm not discussing stealth, I'm
> discussing politics. Keep your orange juice out of my apple cider.

I'm not trying to continue this discussion, I'm merely pointing out that your
insistence that Obfuscate isn't the only stealth discipline, while correct, is
not a very strong argument in practice, because it is the only discipline that
has reasonable stacking of stealth, which is what is required for a stealthy
deck.

I agree that each discipline should maybe be able to do more things, but we
don't need them all to do everything. Disciplines are the different flavors
of the game...sweet, salty, sour, and purple. (It is *too* a flavor!
Haven't you ever had Dimetapp?) Celerity shouldn't taste like Dominate, and
Obfuscate shouldn't taste like Vicissitude. They should each be able to do a
number of things, they should each do a couple of things well. They should
also each do some things poorly. I don't think that you are arguing that
they should all do the same things equally well, but that *is* how it is
coming across.

It is in no way a faulty analogy. Stealth, for the most part, comes from
Obfuscate. There are a few other cards here and there (maybe a card or two in
each of a few disciplines) that also provide stealth. Ok. Good. Now look at
votes. Presence provides the bulk of voting power, but you can still get
voting power elsewhere--Vote cards give you vote power; Bribes give you vote
power; Titled vampires give you vote power; Auspex gives you vote power; Some
locations give you vote power (just like some locations give you stealth
power).

Other disciplines don't need to provide vote power, as there are already plenty
of ways to get votes power that don't require disciplines.

"And without vote pushing, a good Presence voting deck will rip it
apart unless you are using Malk Rider Clauses."

Presence only provides vote power offensively. It helps you pass votes, but it
doesn't help you prevent other folks from passing votes (it can, but if you
start talking about vote defense, then you open up the arena to Surprise
Influence, Pulling Strings, and Delaying Tactics, none of which are Presence
based). Thus, we are talking pure offensiveness. With Presence, you can push
pretty much any vote you want through, true. With Bribes and Titled vampires

crypt has both disciplines, only three of them have both at superior (both of

drawing either all small vampires, none of which have both disciplines or all
huge vampires. Not to say that this isn't a good crypt for a deck that uses

a deck that relies on, say, Obf/Dom, this crypt will be much slower, much less
consistent, and require far more skill cards to be in the deck. As a result,
the Obf/Dom deck is going to be quicker, more reliable, and all around a better
deck.

to be a S+B deck, will probably be a perfectly viable S+B deck, possibly even a
good one, but will be less effective at S+B than a straight Obf/Dom deck. Much
like a non Presence vote deck can be perfectly effective, while still less
effective than a Presence vote deck in a head to head situation. I fail to see

The only one of these decks that I currently have constructed is my
Lasombra deck. For other examples, you could probably check the JOL
archives or regular deck archives.

Lasombra - Core Card: Political Struggle
In case you aren't familiar with it, Political Struggle gives the acting
vampire the ability to attack the target vampire at +1 stealth as a (D)
action. If the target vampire is burned or goes to torpor, burn PS and
the acting vampire gains votes equal to those of the target vampire.

Like many of the non-Presence vote decks I've made, it relies on combat
to eliminate or intimidate oppositional voters. In a four player game,
there is commonly 3 or more other titled vampires in play with my group.
A couple successful Political Struggles and a Power Structure in play
give me vote dominance.

The Lasombra are particularly good at this because they don't require a
ton of cards to send a vampire to Torpor. My group's style allows me to
use Arms of the Abyss, Entombment, and Disarm quite effectively. These
could be adjusted for Thoughts Betrayed and Torn Signpost with Disarm.

Once I have vote dominance through actual votes or negotiation (like I'll
split my KRC's even if you vote with me), I go into stealthy vote mode.
I'll probably modify this deck to remove bleed and add Grave Robbing and
Peace of Khetamon.

Antonio Delgado, Alvaro, and Gratiano are the core vampires. It gets
usually trounced by dedicated rush if that deck doesn't have pressure
from their Predator. Usually, I bring out two of the above vampires plus
Aurora Van Brande and/or Ignacio with a Camarilla Vitae Slave. I also
use Blood Bath and wish I had more than just one.

Other general non-Presence voting decks:
Nosferatu Princes - same principle as Lasombra but more difficult
Weenies with Praxis Seizures - the weenie vote deck is still quite effective,
just harder to build and play
Tremere using Anathema - particularly good in a heavy combat environment

If I also recall correctly, someone had a similar deck to this in the
GenCon finals.

Actually, no. My concern isn't that political decks should be able to
consistently have a "lock down effect." My concern is that political

All of the things you mention are available to decks using Presence,
except Telepathic Vote Counting (unless you play Toreador).

Not necessarily. To begin with, all political actions are at +1 stealth.

to stop votes. Marijava Ghouls with Charming Lobby can give votes extra
stealth.

Besides that, there are four clans that use Presence: Brujah, Setites,
Toreador and Ventrue. Brujah and Toreador can use Alacrity for an extra +1
stealth, Setites have Obfuscate for +1,000,000 stealth, which leaves Ventrue.
While Ventrue don't have stealth, they do have Fortitude and Dominate.
Fortitude can be made to make an action unblockable or Dawn Op/Skin of Steel
to make people think twice about blocking. Dominate has Seduction and
Sleeping Mind to make it difficult to block.

In my mind, that makes the point of stealth moot.

> yes, to have a automatically sucessful vote deck, you need Presence. This is
> not a problem to me.

This, however, _is_ a problem to me. If offensive voting power is more
available to other disciplines, it would lessen the monopoly that Presence
has on voting, making it a more level playing field for voting.
